title: What Smart Utility Management Looks Like
summary: A practical model for smart utility management: collect every bill, check every line item, send clean data to every system, and act on what it shows. See how.
body_markdown:
Utility management is the work of collecting, checking, paying, analyzing, and acting on an organization's utility bills and usage data across every site and every commodity. For a company with dozens or hundreds of locations, that means thousands of bills a year from many different providers, each with its own format, billing cycle, and rate structure.


Most organizations still run this as an accounts payable task: get the bill, pay the bill, file the bill. Smart utility management treats each bill as data. Bills are collected without anyone chasing them, checked line by line, delivered to every team that needs them, and used to make decisions about cost, energy use, and reporting.


Here's what that looks like in practice, how to tell where your organization stands, and where to start.


## The manual baseline


When we ask a multi-site organization how its utility bills are managed, the answer usually involves some mix of utility portals, a shared inbox, paper bills mailed to sites, and a spreadsheet maintained by one or two people. The failure modes are predictable:


- **Missing bills are found late.** A bill that never arrives is noticed when a late fee or disconnection notice shows up, not when it was due.
- **Errors go unchecked.** Estimated reads, wrong rate schedules, and duplicate charges are paid because nobody has time to read every line.
- **Teams use different numbers.** Finance reports costs from the AP system, sustainability reports consumption from a separate spreadsheet, and facilities looks at a third source. Reconciling them takes weeks.
- **Analysis is always behind.** By the time a quarter's data is cleaned up, the chance to act on it has passed.


None of this is a people problem. It's what happens when a high-volume, high-variety data process runs on manual effort.


## Manual vs. smart utility management


- **Collection:** instead of staff logging into portals and forwarding emails, every account is collected automatically from portals, e-bills, and paper.
- **Validation:** instead of spot checks, if any, every line item is checked for anomalies before payment.
- **Payment:** instead of bills keyed into AP with frequent late fees, validated bills are paid on time or sent to AP as coded payables.
- **Analysis:** instead of quarterly spreadsheets, analysis is continuous, at the site, account, and line-item level.
- **Reporting:** instead of each team keeping its own numbers, finance, sustainability, and operations report from one source.
- **Action:** instead of reacting after costs spike, teams act early on rate changes, demand, budgets, and disputes.


## The four stages of smart utility management


We think about smart utility management as four stages: collect, automate, deliver, and act. Each one depends on the one before it.


### 1 Collect every bill, for every account


The foundation is completeness. Every utility account at every site, across every commodity, collected automatically and on time. That includes electricity, natural gas, and water, and it should also include sewer, steam, fuel oil, propane, waste, recycling, and telecom where those bills exist. Nectar covers 9 commodities across more than 7,000 US utilities, with international coverage in more than 5 languages.


Collection should work however bills arrive: utility portals, emailed e-bills, and paper mailed to a site. Site teams should be able to connect accounts through an invitation link without sharing passwords. And the system should notice when a bill that should have arrived hasn't.


### 2 Automate the reading and checking


Once bills are collected, they need to be read at the line-item level. Totals are enough to pay a bill. They aren't enough to check one. Supply charges, delivery charges, demand charges, riders, taxes, and fees each tell you something different.


Nectar's AI parses bills at the line-item level with 99.2% accuracy, with a median processing time under 15 minutes. Every parsed bill is then checked for the issues that cost money: estimated reads, overlapping billing periods, late fees, demand spikes, wrong tariffs, and missing bills. The checks need to separate signal from noise. A system that flags everything gets ignored, so the goal is fewer alerts that are real.


### 3 Deliver clean data to every system


Utility data is used by finance, sustainability, facilities, and leadership, and each group works in different tools. Smart utility management sends the same validated data to all of them:


- **Accounts payable and ERP systems,** as coded payables ready for approval.
- **Carbon accounting platforms,** for Scope 1 and 2 reporting and Scope 3 water and waste.
- **ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager,** for building benchmarking.
- **BI tools and data warehouses,** through exports and an API.


When everyone reports from one source, the reconciliation work disappears and the numbers in the board deck match the numbers in the sustainability report.


### 4 Act on what the data shows


Clean, complete data is the starting point for decisions that reduce cost:


- **Rate and tariff optimization:** finding accounts on schedules that no longer fit their usage, and catching charges that don't match the tariff.
- **Demand management:** using interval data to understand peaks, reduce demand charges, and size projects like batteries.
- **Budgeting and forecasting:** building budgets from line-item history instead of last year's totals.
- **Bill pay:** paying validated bills on time, holding bills with errors, and avoiding late fees entirely.
- **Procurement:** giving brokers and advisors accurate load data for supply contracts in deregulated markets.


Once the data is clean, the total savings opportunity across these areas is typically 11 to 17% of annual utility spend.


## Signs you're there


Use this checklist to see where your organization stands. A smart utility management program can say yes to most of these:


- A missing bill is flagged within days of its expected date.
- Late fees are close to zero.
- Any dollar of utility spend can be traced to a specific line on a specific bill.
- Bills with errors are caught before they're paid.
- Finance and sustainability report the same consumption numbers.
- You know which accounts are on the wrong rate schedule.
- A question about the portfolio gets a cited answer in minutes, not a request to the analyst who owns the spreadsheet.
- The people who used to collect and key in bills now spend that time on analysis and projects.


That last point matters. Operators typically save 5 to 15 hours a week on bill collection and reconciliation alone.


## Where to start


Start with collection and validation. Every later stage depends on complete, accurate data, and most of the immediate savings, such as late fees, billing errors, and wrong tariffs, show up as soon as bills are checked line by line.
